rationale: A wins because it finds the sharper tension: "Klarna won't say how many of the jobs it cut were actually replaced by AI" is a real accountability story, not just a shinier version of the company claim. B is disciplined and useful, but "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is a factual overreach; the update gives average chat resolution time, not dispute-specific outcomes. This is close because B's proof questions are excellent, but A has cleaner structural separation and fewer loaded assumptions.
gaps_in_A: "The most-mocked category of enterprise AI might actually be working" imports a broad industry premise not supplied by the update. It may be a good trend frame, but it needs sourcing.

"Klarna's AI is now handling disputes for a base of 150 million consumers" stretches the facts. Klarna processes payments for 150 million consumers; the update does not say every consumer dispute is AI-handled.
"The figures are surfacing in the same window as Klarna's IPO filing" is slightly slippery. The update says Klarna has filed to go public, not that these exact figures appear in the filing.
"five distinct, journalist-ready shapes exist" oversells readiness. The consumer and contrarian angles still need missing proof before a serious pitch goes out.
gaps_in_B: "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is the biggest miss. The update says average customer-service chat resolution time fell under two minutes, not that disputes are resolved that fast.
"one of the only companies publishing operational numbers" is unsupported. The update does not prove Klarna is rare in the market.
"Klarna is... leading with an AI-efficiency story" may be plausible, but the update does not say the IPO narrative is led by AI.
"How AI actually shrinks a company" overlaps heavily with the data angle. Both lean on the same 700-FTE, hiring-freeze, and headcount facts, so B is a little less distinct than it thinks.
